questions.question: In DSA/ECDSA, what value must never repeat for two signatures made with the same private key?
questions.explanation: Reusing k makes the signature equations solvable for the private key. Many real-world breaks come from RNG or nonce bugs.

questions.question: In ECDSA, the signature arithmetic for r and s is done modulo which value?
questions.explanation: ECDSA works in the subgroup generated by G, whose size is n. The field prime p defines coordinates, not the signature modulus.

questions.question: Which check is the core acceptance condition in ECDSA verification?
options: x(u1·G + u2·Q) mod n equals r
y(u1·G + u2·Q) mod n equals r
x(u1·G + u2·Q) mod p equals r
y(u1·G + u2·Q) mod p equals r
questions.explanation: Verification recomputes an X point from (r, s) and the public key and checks that its x-coordinate matches r modulo n.

questions.question: What practical benefit does RFC 6979-style deterministic k provide?
options: It removes reliance on RNG quality
It reduces signature size on the wire
It converts ECDSA signatures to EdDSA
It eliminates the need for public keys
questions.explanation: Deterministic k uses HMAC over the private key and message hash, so broken randomness does not silently leak the private key.

questions.question: What is the main mathematical difference between DSA and ECDSA group operations?
questions.explanation: DSA works in a subgroup of (Z/pZ)* where the group operation is multiplication, implemented as exponentiation. ECDSA works in an elliptic-curve group using point addition and scalar multiplication.

questions.question: If two ECDSA signatures under the same key reuse the same nonce k, what can an attacker typically do?
questions.explanation: With reused k (often visible as repeated r), the attacker can solve for k and then for the private key using modular inverses.

questions.question: Why do some protocols require low-s ECDSA signatures?
options: To speed up scalar multiplication on curves
To avoid needing a per-signature nonce
questions.explanation: Because (r, s) and (r, n-s) both verify, low-s makes signatures canonical, preventing a simple form of malleability.

questions.question: Which input validation is essential before attempting ECDSA verification?
options: Reject r or s outside the range [1, n-1]
Reject messages longer than the hash size
Reject public keys not on the chosen curve
Reject hashes with too many leading zeros
questions.explanation: If r or s is out of range, the algebra breaks down and edge cases appear. Verifiers should reject invalid ranges before any inversions.
